prompt: What hybridization can the radical carbon of an allyl radical adopt, and where does that put the unpaired electron?

choices.text: sp2, with the unpaired electron in a p orbital
sp3, with the unpaired electron in an sp3 hybrid orbital
choices.why: The radical carbon can adopt sp2 hybridization, which leaves a p orbital to hold the unpaired electron.

choices.text: sp2, with the unpaired electron in an sp2 hybrid orbital
choices.why: The sp2 hybrids form the σ bonds. The unpaired electron goes into the unhybridized p orbital.

choices.text: sp, with the unpaired electron in an sp hybrid orbital
choices.why: The radical carbon is sp2, not sp, and the unpaired electron is in a p orbital.

explanation: The radical carbon can adopt sp2 hybridization, placing the unpaired electron in a p orbital. That p orbital lines up with the p orbitals of the neighboring double bond, giving an electronically symmetrical structure (Figure 10.4.1).

prompt: Which statement about the p orbital on the central carbon of the allyl radical is correct?

choices.text: It overlaps equally well with the p orbitals on both neighboring carbons
It overlaps only with the p orbital of the carbon that carries the unpaired electron
choices.why: The allyl radical is electronically symmetrical, so the central p orbital overlaps equally well on both sides.

choices.text: It holds the unpaired electron
choices.why: The unpaired electron is shared by the two end carbons; the spin-density surface shows it equally on carbons 1 and 3.

choices.text: It doesn't exist, because the central carbon is sp3
choices.why: All three carbons are sp2 with a p orbital, so the π system extends over all three.

explanation: With the radical carbon sp2 hybridized, the allyl radical is electronically symmetrical. The p orbital on the central carbon can therefore overlap equally well with a p orbital on either neighboring carbon, giving rise to two equivalent resonance structures.

prompt: How many resonance forms does the allyl radical have?
explanation: The allyl radical has two resonance forms: one with the unpaired electron on the left and the double bond on the right, and one with the unpaired electron on the right and the double bond on the left. A typical alkyl radical has only a single structure.

prompt: The two resonance forms of the allyl radical are CH2=CH–CH2· and ·CH2–CH=CH2. How do they differ?

choices.text: Only in where the unpaired electron and double bond are drawn
A hydrogen atom moves from one end carbon to the other
choices.why: Resonance forms differ only in the placement of electrons. The atoms, including the hydrogens, stay where they are.

choices.text: One form has the unpaired electron on the central carbon
choices.why: In both forms the unpaired electron is on an end carbon, with the double bond at the other end.

choices.text: One form has two double bonds and the other has none
choices.why: Each form has one double bond and one unpaired electron.

explanation: Because the allyl radical is electronically symmetrical, it has two resonance forms: one with the unpaired electron on the left and the double bond on the right, and one with the unpaired electron on the right and the double bond on the left. Only the electrons are drawn differently.

prompt: Which statement describes the true structure of the allyl radical?

choices.text: It is a resonance hybrid of the two resonance forms
It flips back and forth rapidly between the two resonance forms
choices.why: Neither resonance form is correct by itself. The radical has a single structure, the hybrid, at all times.

choices.text: It is the form with the unpaired electron on the left
choices.why: Neither structure is correct by itself; the two forms are equivalent.

choices.text: It has the unpaired electron on the central carbon
choices.why: The unpaired electron is shared by the two end carbons, not located on the central one.

explanation: Neither resonance structure is correct by itself; the true structure of the allyl radical is a resonance hybrid of the two.

prompt: According to the section, why does a species with more resonance forms tend to be more stable?

choices.text: Its bonding electrons are attracted to more nuclei
Each extra resonance form adds another bond to the molecule
choices.why: Resonance forms are different drawings of the same structure; they don't add bonds.

choices.text: Its electrons are held on a single atom
choices.why: It's the opposite: in the allyl radical the unpaired electron is spread over more than one atom.

choices.text: It spends most of its time in the most stable form
choices.why: The species doesn't switch between forms; its true structure is a hybrid.

explanation: As noted in Section 2.5, the greater the number of resonance forms, the greater the stability of a compound, because bonding electrons are attracted to more nuclei. The allyl radical, with two resonance forms, is therefore more stable than a typical alkyl radical, which has only one structure.

prompt: In molecular orbital terms, why is the allyl radical so stable?

choices.text: Its unpaired electron is delocalized over an extended π-orbital network
Its unpaired electron is localized on the central carbon
choices.why: The electron is spread out, or delocalized, over the π system rather than localized at one site.

choices.text: Its unpaired electron is in an sp3 orbital, held close to the nucleus
choices.why: The unpaired electron is in a p orbital that is part of a π-orbital network.

choices.text: It has no unpaired electron at all
choices.why: The allyl radical is a radical; it has one unpaired electron, delocalized over the π system.

explanation: In molecular orbital terms, the stability of the allyl radical is due to the fact that the unpaired electron is delocalized, or spread out, over an extended π-orbital network rather than localized at only one site (Figure 10.4.2).

prompt: What does the spin-density surface of the allyl radical show about the unpaired electron?

choices.text: The two terminal carbons share it equally
It sits mostly on the central carbon
choices.why: The spin-density surface shows the unpaired electron on the two terminal carbons, not the central one.

choices.text: It sits on just one terminal carbon
choices.why: Both terminal carbons share the unpaired electron, and they share it equally.

choices.text: It sits on the hydrogen atoms
choices.why: The unpaired electron is in the carbon π system, shared by the two end carbons.

explanation: The spin-density surface shows the calculated location of the unpaired electron. It is equally shared between the two terminal carbons of the allyl radical (Figure 10.4.2).

prompt: Why does allylic bromination of an unsymmetrical alkene often give a mixture of products?

choices.text: Br2 can react at either end of the delocalized allylic radical
NBS adds bromine to both carbons of the double bond
choices.why: NBS doesn't add across the double bond; it substitutes an allylic hydrogen.

choices.text: Both the allylic and the vinylic hydrogens are replaced
choices.why: Vinylic C–H bonds are too strong to be broken; only allylic hydrogens are abstracted.

choices.text: The bromoalkene product rearranges through a carbocation
choices.why: The mixture comes from the delocalized radical, not from a carbocation rearrangement.

explanation: Because the unpaired electron is delocalized over both ends of the π orbital system, reaction with Br2 can occur at either end. With an unsymmetrical alkene the two ends differ, so a mixture of products often forms.

prompt: Which products form when 1-octene reacts with NBS?

choices.text: 3-bromo-1-octene and 1-bromo-2-octene
3-bromo-1-octene only
choices.why: The allylic radical's unpaired electron is shared by carbons 1 and 3, so bromine can end up at either carbon.

choices.text: 1,2-dibromooctane only
choices.why: That would be the Br2 addition product. NBS substitutes an allylic hydrogen.

choices.text: 3-bromo-1-octene and 4-bromo-2-octene
choices.why: Carbon 4 isn't part of the allylic system. The radical's two ends are carbons 1 and 3.

explanation: Removing an allylic hydrogen from carbon 3 of 1-octene gives an allylic radical with its unpaired electron shared by carbons 1 and 3. Bromine at carbon 3 gives 3-bromo-1-octene (17%); bromine at carbon 1, with the double bond moved to carbons 2–3, gives 1-bromo-2-octene (83%).

prompt: Bromination of 1-octene with NBS gives 3-bromo-1-octene and 1-bromo-2-octene. What percentage of the product mixture is 1-bromo-2-octene?
explanation: The section reports 17% 3-bromo-1-octene and 83% 1-bromo-2-octene. The two products aren't formed in equal amounts because reaction at the less hindered, primary end of the allylic radical is favored.

prompt: Why is 1-bromo-2-octene formed in larger amount than 3-bromo-1-octene from 1-octene and NBS?

choices.text: Reaction at the radical's less hindered, primary end is favored
The unpaired electron is found only on carbon 1, never on carbon 3
choices.why: The unpaired electron is delocalized over both ends; reaction at carbon 1 is simply favored because it is less hindered.

choices.text: The secondary end of the radical is the less hindered end
choices.why: The primary end (carbon 1) is the less hindered one, and that is where reaction is favored.

choices.text: The C–H bonds on carbon 1 are the weakest in the molecule
choices.why: Carbon 1 is vinylic in 1-octene; its C–H bonds are strong. The hydrogen removed is the allylic one on carbon 3.

explanation: The intermediate allylic radical from 1-octene is not symmetrical, so reaction at its two ends is not equally likely. Reaction at the less hindered, primary end is favored, giving 83% 1-bromo-2-octene and 17% 3-bromo-1-octene.

prompt: In the bromination of 1-octene with NBS, 1-bromo-2-octene makes up 83% of the product and forms as a 53 : 47 mixture of trans and cis isomers. What percentage of the total product is trans-1-bromo-2-octene, to the nearest whole percent?
explanation: The trans isomer is 53% of the 83%: 0.53 × 83% = 44% of the total product. The cis isomer makes up 0.47 × 83% = 39%, and 3-bromo-1-octene the remaining 17%.

prompt: 3-Bromocyclohexene, made from cyclohexene and NBS, is treated with the base KOH. What forms?

choices.text: 1,3-cyclohexadiene
1,4-cyclohexadiene
choices.why: Dehydrohalogenation removes H and Br from neighboring carbons, so the new double bond includes carbon 3, right next to the old one. That gives the 1,3-diene.

choices.text: Cyclohexene
choices.why: KOH doesn't supply a hydrogen to replace the bromine; it removes HBr to make a second double bond.

choices.text: Benzene
choices.why: Losing one HBr adds only one double bond, giving a diene, not benzene's three double bonds.

explanation: The products of allylic bromination are useful for conversion into dienes by dehydrohalogenation with base. Cyclohexene gives 3-bromocyclohexene with NBS, and KOH then converts that into 1,3-cyclohexadiene.

prompt: Not counting stereoisomers, how many different products form when 4,4-dimethylcyclohexene reacts with NBS (Worked Example 10.4.1)?
explanation: There are two different allylic positions, carbons 3 and 6, and each allylic radical can add Br at either end, for up to four products. The two products from the radical at carbon 6 are identical, so only three form: 3-bromo-4,4-dimethylcyclohexene, 6-bromo-3,3-dimethylcyclohexene and 3-bromo-5,5-dimethylcyclohexene.

prompt: 4,4-Dimethylcyclohexene has two different allylic positions, and each allylic radical can react at either end, so up to four products could form with NBS. Why do only three form?

choices.text: Both ends of the radical formed at carbon 6 give the same compound
One allylic carbon, carbon 3, has no hydrogens to abstract
choices.why: Carbons 3 and 6 are both CH2 groups. The carbon with no hydrogens is carbon 4, which isn't allylic.

choices.text: The radical formed at carbon 3 can react at only one end
choices.why: Each allylic radical can add Br at either end. The radical at carbon 3 gives two different products.

choices.text: One of the four is a vinylic bromide, which doesn't form
choices.why: None of the four possible products is vinylic; they come from two allylic radicals, each reacting at two ends.

explanation: Abstracting a hydrogen from each of the two allylic positions gives two allylic radicals, each of which can add Br at either end. The radical at carbon 3 gives 3-bromo-4,4-dimethylcyclohexene and 6-bromo-3,3-dimethylcyclohexene. Both ends of the radical at carbon 6 give the same compound, 3-bromo-5,5-dimethylcyclohexene, so only three products form.

prompt: Which compound is one of the products of 4,4-dimethylcyclohexene with NBS?

choices.text: 3-bromo-5,5-dimethylcyclohexene
5-bromo-4,4-dimethylcyclohexene
choices.why: That has bromine on carbon 5, which isn't next to the double bond, so it isn't allylic.

choices.text: 1-bromo-4,4-dimethylcyclohexene
choices.why: That would replace a vinylic hydrogen, which NBS doesn't do.

choices.text: trans-1,2-dibromo-4,4-dimethylcyclohexane
choices.why: That is a Br2 addition product. NBS substitutes an allylic hydrogen and leaves a double bond in the product.

explanation: The three products are 3-bromo-4,4-dimethylcyclohexene and 6-bromo-3,3-dimethylcyclohexene (from the radical at carbon 3) and 3-bromo-5,5-dimethylcyclohexene (from the radical at carbon 6), as worked out in Worked Example 10.4.1.

prompt: The cyclohexadienyl radical is a six-membered ring of one CH2 carbon and five CH carbons; the five CH carbons share two C=C bonds and one unpaired electron. How many resonance forms can be drawn for it?
explanation: The unpaired electron can sit on either carbon next to the CH2 group or on the middle carbon of the five-carbon π system, with the two double bonds shifting each time. Exercise 10.4.1 asks for these three resonance forms.

prompt: Methylenecyclohexane, a cyclohexane ring with a =CH2 group on one ring carbon, reacts with NBS to give mainly 1-(bromomethyl)cyclohexene. Why?

choices.text: The radical reacts at its more accessible end, giving the more substituted C=C
NBS replaces a vinylic hydrogen of the =CH2 group with bromine
choices.why: Vinylic hydrogens aren't removed. A ring allylic hydrogen is abstracted, and Br ends up at the CH2 end of the allylic radical.

choices.text: Br2 adds across the C=CH2 double bond of the starting alkene
choices.why: Adding Br2 would give a dibromide with no double bond. NBS substitutes an allylic hydrogen instead.

choices.text: The radical's unpaired electron is located only on the CH2 carbon
choices.why: The unpaired electron is delocalized over both ends of the allylic radical; the CH2 end is favored because it is more accessible.

explanation: Removing an allylic ring hydrogen gives an allylic radical with one end on the ring carbon and the other on the CH2 carbon. Reaction at the more accessible CH2 end puts Br there and moves the double bond into the ring, giving the more highly substituted double bond of 1-(bromomethyl)cyclohexene (Exercise 10.4.2).

prompt: 2-Methyl-3-hexene, (CH3)2CHCH=CHCH2CH3, reacts with NBS. Counting constitutional isomers only (ignore E/Z and other stereoisomers), how many different products would you expect?
explanation: There are two allylic positions, carbon 2 and carbon 5, and each allylic radical can add Br at either end. That gives four products: 2-bromo-2-methyl-3-hexene, 4-bromo-2-methyl-2-hexene, 2-bromo-5-methyl-3-hexene and 4-bromo-5-methyl-2-hexene (Exercise 10.4.3b).
